title: Myanmar Shows War Doesn’t Stop Mining
gist: Myanmar—supplying an estimated 16% of global rare-earth output and nearly half of global heavy rare earths critical to defense and green tech—shows that China-centered supply chains adapt to civil war rather than break, with the Kachin Independence Army's 2024 seizure of the Pangwa mining hub merely changing who controls extraction while production continues and pollution spreads into Thailand.

insights.claim: Myanmar accounts for an estimated 16 percent of global rare-earth mining output and may supply nearly half of global heavy rare-earth production—critical for defense and green energy—most extracted in Kachin and shipped to China for processing.
insights.speaker: Kristina Kironska, Jan-Sha
insights.so_what: Concentration of heavy-rare-earth supply in a single conflict zone feeding China is a structural chokepoint for defense and clean-energy manufacturers worldwide.
insights.quote: it may supplies nearly half of global production of heavy rare earths, which are critical for the defense industry and green energy
insights.locator: Myanmar accounts for an estimated 16 percent

insights.claim: The Kachin Independence Army seized Pangwa, the hub of Kachin's rare-earth industry, from military-affiliated militia in 2024, but production continued almost unimpeded—control of a critical supply-chain point simply changed hands.
insights.speaker: Kristina Kironska, Jan-Sha
insights.so_what: Demonstrates rare-earth supply resilience to territorial upheaval, meaning conflict-driven supply disruptions may be less likely than markets assume.
insights.quote: instead of severing the supply chain, it simply put control of a critical point in new hands. Production has continued almost unimpeded.
insights.locator: The Kachin Independence Army, one of many groups

insights.claim: Beijing does not rely solely on Myanmar's central government but engages military authorities, ethnic armed organizations, militias, borderland elites, and business intermediaries, so conflict changes who controls and profits from extraction rather than stopping it.
insights.speaker: Kristina Kironska, Jan-Sha
insights.so_what: China's multi-actor engagement strategy insulates its critical-mineral access from regime change, a durable advantage in contested resource geographies.
insights.quote: Conflict does not stop extraction; it changes who controls it, who profits from it, and who bears its costs.
insights.locator: Beijing does not rely solely on Myanmar’s central government.

insights.claim: As China tightened domestic environmental regulation from the 2010s, the most damaging rare-earth mining shifted to northern Myanmar, where minerals are then mixed with material from other sources during transport and refining, making origin nearly impossible to trace.
insights.speaker: Kristina Kironska, Jan-Sha
insights.so_what: Origin-obscuring supply chains mean 'clean' green-tech products may embed conflict minerals, undermining ESG claims and traceability mandates.
insights.quote: making it extremely difficult for governments, manufacturers, or consumers to determine the origin of the components used in technologies that are marketed as part of the green transition
insights.locator: Heavy rare earths are both strategically indispensable

insights.claim: KIO control of Kachin's rare-earth industry finances its military operations and public services but has raised production costs, pushing Chinese investors to cut labor costs or relocate to Shan state areas controlled by the TNLA, UWSA, and NDAA, and near Thailand and Laos.
insights.speaker: Kristina Kironska, Jan-Sha
insights.so_what: Rising extraction costs and geographic dispersal of mining signal shifting cost bases and new pollution fronts to track in rare-earth supply.
insights.quote: Chinese investors are cutting labor costs or moving to other locations in Shan state
insights.locator: The KIO now controls Kachin state’s rare-earth industry

insights.claim: The dominant in-situ leaching method injects chemicals into the ground and has polluted tributaries of the Mekong, Irrawaddy, and Salween; northern Thailand's Kok River showed extremely high arsenic levels, prompting a protest outside the Chinese Consulate in Chiang Mai that police dispersed, injuring two.
insights.speaker: Kristina Kironska, Jan-Sha
insights.so_what: Cross-border pollution is generating diplomatic friction with Thailand, a reputational and regulatory risk that could pressure the supply chain.
insights.quote: the Kok River was found to contain extremely high levels of arsenic
insights.locator: The most common extraction method, in-situ leaching

insights.claim: Local communities bear long-term environmental costs while Chinese investors capture most profits, with accountability mechanisms weak or absent—a dynamic also seen at the Letpadaung copper mine and the oil and gas pipelines that resumed under military protection after the 2021 coup.
insights.speaker: Kristina Kironska, Jan-Sha
insights.so_what: Persistent Chinese extraction through coup and civil war shows the resilience and adaptability of China-linked infrastructure in Myanmar.
insights.quote: Local communities bear the long-term environmental costs while Chinese investors capture most of the profits.
insights.locator: Communities living near mining areas bear the brunt.

themes.theme: An emerging model of conflict extraction

insights.claim: Myanmar mirrors eastern Congo, where M23's 2024 capture of the Rubaya coltan mining area did not halt the trade but saw the group monopolize exports through Rwanda—illustrating a pattern where territorial control changes without severing the commodity chain.
insights.speaker: Kristina Kironska, Jan-Sha
insights.so_what: A generalizable 21st-century model: strategic supply chains adapt to and depend on wartime fragmented authority, reshaping how minerals-supply risk should be assessed.
insights.quote: As in Myanmar, territorial control changed without severing the commodity chain.
insights.locator: A similar dynamic is visible in eastern Congo

insights.claim: The author argues Western governments demand 'clean' supply chains while remaining structurally dependent on extraction systems embedded in civil war that they have little ability or willingness to regulate, so conflict must be treated as part of supply-chain governance.
insights.speaker: Kristina Kironska, Jan-Sha
insights.so_what: Highlights a gap between Western ESG rhetoric and dependence on conflict extraction, a policy and compliance exposure for green-tech and defense buyers.
insights.quote: Western governments increasingly demand “clean” supply chains while remaining structurally dependent on extraction systems that they have little ability, or willingness, to regulate.
insights.locator: Together, Myanmar and eastern Congo illustrate a broader pattern
